patient.name: Bernadette O'Sullivan
patient.complaint: Tiredness, weight gain and always feeling cold for 6 months
background: Heavy periods for the last year
Takes insulin and ferrous sulphate (started by another GP)

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and bradycardia, often in a woman with another autoimmune disease, or 'most likely finding on examination' (slow-relaxing reflexes).

points: Gained 6 kg without eating more; wears a cardigan in July.
Constipated, low mood, struggling to concentrate at work.
Periods heavier; hair coming out in the shower.

steps.lead: Everything Bernadette describes is a body **running slow**: too little thyroid hormone lowers the metabolic rate in almost every tissue.

points: Dry, cool skin; **outer third of both eyebrows missing**.
Puffy around the eyes; voice slightly hoarse.
Tapping her wrist gives tingling in the fingers (Tinel's positive).

steps.lead: Bernadette has the full picture: fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, menorrhagia, bradycardia, **Hertoghe sign**, slow-relaxing reflexes and even carpal tunnel.

steps.q: Which examination finding is most specific for hypothyroidism here?
o: Delayed relaxation of the ankle jerks
steps.r: **Slow-relaxing deep tendon reflexes** are the classic exam sign. Bradycardia, dry skin and low mood all have many other causes.

steps.lead: In London, iodine deficiency is unlikely. A woman with **type 1 diabetes** points straight to autoimmune **Hashimoto's**. Always scan the drug list for amiodarone or lithium.
Bernadette's type 1 diabetes is the **most common autoimmune association** (shared HLA-DR3). Her goitre fits Hashimoto's lymphocytic infiltration.

steps.text: Autoimmune clusters: a stem with **type 1 diabetes, vitiligo, coeliac or Addison's** plus tiredness and weight gain is hypothyroidism until proven otherwise.

steps.lead: If Bernadette went untreated, or stopped her tablets and caught an infection in winter, she could slide into **myxoedema coma**: hypothermic, bradycardic, hypotensive and drowsy.

steps.text: Do not call a raised TSH with normal T4 'hypothyroidism' in an asymptomatic patient. That is **subclinical hypothyroidism**, a separate exam answer.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (TFTs), interpreting a TSH/free T4 pattern, and when to recheck TFTs after a dose change (4 to 6 weeks).

steps.q: What single test confirms Bernadette's suspected diagnosis?
o: Thyroid function tests (TSH and free T4)
steps.r: **TFTs** are the gold standard. Imaging is for lumps and hyperthyroidism, not for diagnosing an underactive gland.

steps.title: Bernadette's bloods
steps.text: High TSH, low free T4, anti-TPO positive: primary hypothyroidism from Hashimoto's. Low MCV and ferritin: co-existing iron deficiency.

steps.lead: Bernadette's **high TSH with low free T4** is the primary pattern. A high TSH with a normal T4 would be subclinical.

visual.title: TSH
visual.label: Bernadette 18.4
visual.caption: TSH is the most sensitive test: the pituitary shouts louder when the thyroid fails.

steps.text: Read TSH first, then free T4 to tell overt from subclinical.

steps.lead: Once Bernadette starts levothyroxine, her TSH needs **4–6 weeks** to settle, so that is when her TFTs are rechecked after every dose change.

visual.title: Bernadette's TSH on levothyroxine
visual.caption: Checked every 6 weeks, the dose stepped up each time TSH was still high.

steps.text: Rechecking TFTs **one week** after a dose change is a classic wrong answer. TSH has not had time to change; wait **4–6 weeks**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?' (levothyroxine, not carbimazole or liothyronine), dose cautions in the elderly and IHD, the iron interaction, pregnancy, and myxoedema coma.

steps.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment for Bernadette?
steps.r: Overt primary hypothyroidism is treated with **levothyroxine** (synthetic T4). Carbimazole treats an overactive gland.

steps.lead: Bernadette starts **levothyroxine** with dose titration by TSH. Starting **low** matters most in the elderly and in ischaemic heart disease, where a big dose can trigger angina.

points: Twelve weeks in, TSH is still higher than expected.
She swallows levothyroxine **with her ferrous sulphate** at breakfast.
Still breathless on stairs; Hb 108 g/L, MCV 74 fL.

steps.lead: Iron is blocking Bernadette's levothyroxine absorption. Levothyroxine goes first, iron **2–4 hours later**. Her low MCV also needs its own iron-deficiency work-up.

visual.title: Subclinical hypothyroidism: TSH decides
visual.label: Example 7.5
visual.caption: Between 5.5 and 10: over 80s watch-and-wait; under 65 with symptoms and two raised TSHs, 6-month trial.

steps.text: If Bernadette's T4 had been normal, this is how the decision would go.
Pregnancy: **increase levothyroxine by 25 mcg** as soon as pregnancy is confirmed and recheck TFTs in **4 weeks**.

points: Three winters later, after a bereavement, she **stops her tablets**.
Neighbour finds her confused, cold and slow to answer.

visual.title: Core temperature
visual.label: Bernadette 33.9
visual.caption: Hypothermia plus bradycardia, hypotension and drowsiness: myxoedema coma.

steps.q: Which is the most appropriate management now?
o: ICU, IV hydrocortisone and IV levothyroxine
Oral levothyroxine 25 mcg and ward review
Restart her old oral dose at home
steps.r: **Myxoedema coma** is an emergency: ICU, **IV hydrocortisone** plus **IV levothyroxine**, supportive care and senior endocrine input.

steps.lead: Bernadette goes to ICU. **Hydrocortisone** is given until adrenal insufficiency is excluded, because thyroid hormone in untreated Addison's can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Bernadette's care follows **NICE NG145**: TFTs to diagnose, levothyroxine titrated to TSH, rechecked every 4–6 weeks after a change.

science.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely mechanism...?' for Hashimoto's (anti-TPO antibodies, lymphocytic destruction), the raised TSH (lost negative feedback), or a sign such as bradycardia.

steps.title: The thyroid axis in Bernadette
steps.caption: Primary failure = high TSH. A pituitary cause would give a low TSH.

steps.lead: Bernadette's TSH of 18.4 is the pituitary responding to the **loss of negative feedback** from low T4.
Bernadette's anti-TPO antibodies mark the autoimmune attack. Some patients have a brief **hashitoxicosis** first, as damaged follicles leak stored hormone.

steps.q: What is the main mechanism of Bernadette's thyroid failure?
o: Lymphocytic infiltration and follicular cell destruction
steps.r: Hashimoto's is **autoimmune destruction**: anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies with lymphocytic infiltration. TSH receptor stimulation is Graves'.

steps.lead: Bernadette's **54 bpm**, constipation and slow-relaxing ankle jerks all come from less thyroid hormone acting on heart, gut and muscle.
Stopping her tablets plus a **chest infection** and **cold** weather tipped Bernadette into decompensated, multi-organ hypometabolism.

steps.text: Hertoghe sign, goitre and periorbital puffiness come from the slow build-up of **myxoedema**: glycosaminoglycan deposits in skin and soft tissue.

mcq.q: What is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in the UK?
mcq.r: In developed countries Hashimoto's (anti-TPO positive) is most common; iodine deficiency is most common worldwide.

mcq.q: What is the Hertoghe (Queen Anne's) sign?
o: Loss of the lateral third of the eyebrows
mcq.r: Hertoghe sign is loss of the outer third of the eyebrows.

mcq.q: Which autoimmune condition is most commonly associated with Hashimoto's?
mcq.r: Type 1 diabetes is the most common association (shared HLA-DR3/DR5).

mcq.q: What TFT pattern defines subclinical hypothyroidism?
mcq.r: Subclinical: TSH raised, free T4 normal, usually no symptoms.

mcq.q: When should TFTs be rechecked after a levothyroxine dose change?
mcq.r: TSH takes 4–6 weeks to reach a new steady state.

mcq.q: How far apart should levothyroxine and ferrous sulphate be taken?
mcq.r: Iron reduces levothyroxine absorption: levothyroxine first, iron 2–4 hours later.

mcq.q: A woman on levothyroxine has a positive pregnancy test. What should happen to her dose?
o: No change until the second trimester
mcq.r: Increase by 25 mcg as soon as pregnancy is confirmed and recheck TFTs in 4 weeks.

mcq.q: Which is given alongside IV levothyroxine in myxoedema coma?
mcq.r: IV hydrocortisone until adrenal insufficiency is excluded.

mcq.q: Why is TSH raised in primary hypothyroidism?
o: Loss of negative feedback from low T4
mcq.r: Low T4 removes negative feedback on the pituitary, so TSH rises.

technique.stem: A 47 year old woman has a 5 month history of fatigue, constipation and 5 kg weight gain. She feels cold all the time and her periods have become heavier. She has vitiligo. Her pulse rate is 56 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg. She has dry skin and a small diffuse non-tender goitre. Her ankle reflexes relax slowly.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question: decide whether the body is running slow or fast.

clues: fatigue, constipation and 5 kg weight gain
steps.x: Every symptom is hypometabolic. Vitiligo marks an autoimmune tendency; goitre plus slow reflexes point to the thyroid.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Autoimmune primary hypothyroidism with goitre: **Hashimoto's thyroiditis**.

elim: Addison's causes weight loss, hyperpigmentation and hypotension, not weight gain and goitre.
Depression does not cause bradycardia, goitre or slow-relaxing reflexes.
Graves' is hyperthyroid: weight loss, heat intolerance, tachycardia.
Iron deficiency explains fatigue but not cold intolerance, goitre or slow reflexes.

steps.x: **D. Hashimoto's thyroiditis.** Slow everything plus goitre plus another autoimmune disease = Hashimoto's.

technique.stem: A 39 year old woman has felt tired for 3 months. She has no other symptoms and examination is normal. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg. Routine bloods show a TSH of 7.2 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 of 13 pmol/L (9–23). Repeat TFTs 3 months later are unchanged.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

steps.x: Next investigation: first name the TFT pattern.

clues: Repeat TFTs 3 months later are unchanged
steps.x: Raised TSH with normal T4, persistent on repeat: **subclinical hypothyroidism**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: First-line further test in subclinical disease is **TPO antibodies**: positive means Hashimoto's and a higher risk of progression.

elim: Free T3 adds nothing when T4 is normal and TSH is raised.
Synacthen tests adrenal function; nothing suggests Addison's.
Isotope scans are for hyperthyroidism and hot nodules.
Ultrasound is for a palpable nodule or lump; her neck is normal.

steps.x: **D. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies.** Subclinical: repeat TFTs in 3–6 months, then check anti-TPO.

technique.stem: An 81 year old man with ischaemic heart disease has had 6 months of tiredness and constipation. He had a myocardial infarction 4 years ago and has stable angina. His pulse rate is 52 bpm and BP 146/82 mmHg. Investigations show TSH 24 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 5.1 pmol/L (9–23).
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Watch and wait with repeat TFTs in 6 months

steps.x: Initial management: diagnose, then check who the patient is.
Overt primary hypothyroidism in an elderly man with **IHD**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Levothyroxine, started **low (25 mcg)** and titrated slowly to avoid angina and arrhythmia.

elim: Carbimazole treats hyperthyroidism.
A full weight-based dose risks angina and arrhythmia in IHD.
Liothyronine (T3) is not first-line and acts fast, stressing the heart.
Watch-and-wait is for over 80s with TSH 5.5–10 and normal T4, not overt disease.

steps.x: **C. Levothyroxine 25 micrograms daily.** Elderly or IHD: start low, go slow, recheck in 4–6 weeks.

technique.stem: A 34 year old woman has a 4 month history of tiredness and weight gain. Her pulse rate is 58 bpm. She has a firm, painless, diffuse goitre. Investigations show a raised TSH, low free T4 and strongly positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her thyroid failure?
o: Granulomatous inflammation after a viral illness
Lymphocytic infiltration with destruction of follicular cells

steps.x: Mechanism: name the disease, then how it works.
Primary hypothyroidism with goitre and anti-TPO: **Hashimoto's**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Autoimmune **lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltration** destroying follicles; the infiltrate makes the goitre.

elim: TSH receptor stimulation causes Graves' hyperthyroidism.
De Quervain's is painful and follows a viral illness.
Iodine deficiency is the worldwide cause but is not antibody-positive.
Pituitary failure gives a low TSH, not a raised one.

steps.x: **D. Lymphocytic infiltration with destruction of follicular cells.** Anti-TPO plus goitre plus high TSH = Hashimoto's.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman has a 6 month history of tiredness, cold intolerance and hair thinning. She has gained 7 kg. She has type 1 diabetes. Her temperature is 36.2°C, pulse rate 55 bpm and BP 134/86 mmHg. She has dry skin, periorbital puffiness and loss of the lateral third of her eyebrows.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Cold intolerance, weight gain, bradycardia and Hertoghe sign in a woman with type 1 diabetes is autoimmune hypothyroidism. Nephrotic syndrome gives puffiness but not cold intolerance or eyebrow loss.

steps.x: Diagnosis: slow or fast metabolism?

clues: loss of the lateral third of her eyebrows
steps.x: Hypometabolic picture, Hertoghe sign and an autoimmune background.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hashimoto's thyroiditis** (autoimmune primary hypothyroidism).

elim: Addison's causes weight loss and hypotension.
Cushing's gives central obesity, striae and hypertension, not bradycardia and cold intolerance.
Nephrotic syndrome causes oedema but not eyebrow loss or bradycardia.
PCOS causes irregular periods and hirsutism, not cold intolerance.

steps.x: **C. Hashimoto's thyroiditis.** Hertoghe sign plus type 1 diabetes is the autoimmune thyroid clue.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman has felt slow and tired for 8 months. She is constipated and her voice has become hoarse. Her pulse rate is 52 bpm and BP 140/90 mmHg. Investigations show a TSH of 21 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 of 5.8 pmol/L (9–23).
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Delayed relaxation of the ankle reflexes
Fine tremor of the outstretched hands
practice.e: Hypothyroidism slows neuromuscular reflex relaxation, giving slow-relaxing ankle jerks. Tremor, lid lag and exophthalmos are hyperthyroid or Graves' signs.

steps.x: Examination finding: first make the diagnosis from the bloods.
High TSH, low T4: primary hypothyroidism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The classic sign: **delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes**.

elim: Clonus is an upper motor neuron sign.
Exophthalmos is Graves' eye disease.
Fine tremor is hyperthyroid.
Lid lag is a sign of thyrotoxicosis.

steps.x: **B. Delayed relaxation of the ankle reflexes.** Slow gland, slow reflexes.

practice.stem: A 76 year old woman is brought to the Emergency Department in January, confused and drowsy. She has hypothyroidism but stopped her tablets 2 months ago. She has a productive cough. Her temperature is 33.4°C, pulse rate 40 bpm, BP 82/48 mmHg and respiratory rate 8 breaths per minute. She has periorbital oedema, sparse hair and absent reflexes.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, reduced consciousness and hyporeflexia after stopping levothyroxine, precipitated by infection and cold, is myxoedema coma. Sepsis is the trigger, not the whole picture.

steps.x: Diagnosis: an emergency in a known thyroid patient.
Cold, infection and stopping replacement: the three classic precipitants. Everything is slowed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Myxoedema coma**: decompensated hypothyroidism.

elim: Addisonian crisis is not hypothermic and bradycardic with a TSH of 68.
Glucose of 3.6 is too mild to explain coma, and does not explain hypothermia or bradycardia.
Septic shock is tachycardic; infection here is the precipitant.
Thyroid storm is hyperthermic and tachycardic.

steps.x: **C. Myxoedema coma.** Hypothermia + bradycardia + coma in a hypothyroid patient off treatment.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has a 3 month history of tiredness, weight gain and constipation. He has atrial fibrillation treated with amiodarone for the past year. His pulse rate is 58 bpm irregularly irregular and BP 128/80 mmHg. Investigations show a TSH of 16 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 of 7 pmol/L (9–23).
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his hypothyroidism?
practice.e: Amiodarone is iodine-rich and a recognised cause of hypothyroidism (as is lithium). A pituitary cause would give a low TSH.

steps.x: Cause question: the drug list is usually the answer.
Primary hypothyroidism developing on amiodarone.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Drug-induced** (amiodarone) hypothyroidism.

elim: Iodine deficiency is a worldwide cause; amiodarone is an iodine excess.
Pituitary disease gives low or normal TSH.
Post-viral thyroiditis follows a painful viral illness.
Thyroid lymphoma presents as a rapidly enlarging neck mass.

steps.x: **A. Drug-induced.** Always scan the drug list for amiodarone and lithium.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has a routine health check. She feels well and has no symptoms. Examination is normal. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. Investigations show a TSH of 6.8 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 of 14 pmol/L (9–23).
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Raised TSH with normal free T4 and no symptoms is subclinical hypothyroidism. Overt primary disease needs a low free T4.

steps.x: Diagnosis from a TFT pattern.
TSH high, T4 normal, asymptomatic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Subclinical hypothyroidism**: repeat TFTs in 3–6 months and check TPO antibodies.

elim: Primary hypothyroidism needs a low free T4.
Secondary disease has a low or normal TSH.
Sick euthyroid occurs in acutely ill patients; she is well.
Subclinical hyperthyroidism has a low TSH.

steps.x: **E. Subclinical hypothyroidism.** High TSH + normal T4 + no symptoms.

practice.stem: A 50 year old woman has 2 months of tingling in her right thumb, index and middle fingers, worse at night. Tapping over her wrist reproduces it. She also reports tiredness, heavy periods and weight gain. Her pulse rate is 54 bpm and BP 136/88 mmHg. Her skin is dry and her ankle reflexes relax slowly.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her hand symptoms?
practice.e: Carpal tunnel syndrome (positive Tinel's) is a recognised association of hypothyroidism; her bradycardia, menorrhagia, weight gain and slow reflexes confirm it.

steps.x: Underlying cause: name the hand problem, then what drives it.

clues: Tapping over her wrist reproduces it
steps.x: Median nerve distribution with positive Tinel's: carpal tunnel. Systemic slow features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Carpal tunnel syndrome caused by **hypothyroidism**.

elim: Acromegaly causes carpal tunnel but with coarse features and large hands, not bradycardia.
Radiculopathy follows a dermatome with neck pain; Tinel's at the wrist points to the carpal tunnel.
RA would cause joint swelling and morning stiffness.
B12 deficiency gives a symmetrical sensory neuropathy, not median-nerve tingling.

steps.x: **C. Hypothyroidism.** Carpal tunnel plus slow features = check the thyroid.

practice.stem: A 61 year old woman has a 4 month history of fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation. Her temperature is 36.0°C, pulse rate 56 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. She has dry skin and slow-relaxing reflexes.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: TFTs (TSH and free T4) are the gold standard and first test for suspected hypothyroidism. Antibodies find the cause once TFTs are abnormal.

steps.x: Initial investigation for a suspected diagnosis.
Classic hypothyroid picture.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thyroid function tests.**

elim: Cortisol tests for Addison's, which causes weight loss.
Isotope scans assess hyperthyroidism and nodules.
Antibodies come after abnormal TFTs, to find the cause.
Ultrasound is for a lump, not for gland function.

steps.x: **B. Thyroid function tests.** Function first, cause second.

practice.stem: A 55 year old woman has primary hypothyroidism. Her levothyroxine dose was increased from 75 to 100 micrograms daily because her TSH was 8.4 mU/L (0.4–4.0). She feels a little better. Her pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
practice.q: When should her thyroid function tests next be checked?
practice.e: TSH has a half-life of 4–6 weeks, so TFTs are rechecked 4–6 weeks after any dose change. One week is too early to show the new steady state.

steps.x: Timing of monitoring after a dose change.

clues: dose was increased from 75 to 100 micrograms daily
steps.x: A dose has just changed; the next TSH tells you if it is right.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **4–6 weeks**, because of the TSH half-life.

elim: One week is too soon; TSH will not have settled.
Six months leaves her under-treated for too long.
Annual checks are for a stable dose.
Titration is guided by TSH, not symptoms alone.

steps.x: **B. In 4–6 weeks.** Every dose change: recheck at 4–6 weeks.

practice.stem: A 49 year old woman has hypothyroidism and iron deficiency anaemia. Her TSH remains raised despite two dose increases, and she says she takes all her tablets. She takes levothyroxine and ferrous sulphate together every morning with breakfast. Her pulse rate is 62 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Take levothyroxine first and ferrous sulphate 4 hours later
practice.e: Ferrous sulphate reduces levothyroxine absorption; spacing them (levothyroxine first, iron 2–4 hours later) fixes the problem. Stopping iron leaves her anaemia untreated.

steps.x: Next step: why is TSH still high?

clues: TSH remains raised despite two dose increases
steps.x: Adherent, but taking iron with levothyroxine: an absorption interaction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Separate the tablets: **levothyroxine first, iron 2–4 hours later**.

elim: Liothyronine is not used to fix poor absorption.
Raising the dose ignores the cause.
Her iron deficiency still needs treating.
Carbimazole is for hyperthyroidism.

steps.x: **E. Space the doses.** Iron, calcium and HRT all reduce levothyroxine absorption.

practice.stem: A 31 year old woman with Hashimoto's thyroiditis takes levothyroxine 100 micrograms daily. Her last TFTs were normal. She has just had a positive pregnancy test at 5 weeks. She is well. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Continue the same dose and check TFTs at 20 weeks
Increase levothyroxine by 25 micrograms and check TFTs in 4 weeks
practice.e: Requirements rise in pregnancy, so NICE advises increasing by 25 micrograms as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, even if euthyroid, with TFTs in 4 weeks.

steps.x: Next step in a pregnant woman on levothyroxine.
Euthyroid on treatment and newly pregnant.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Increase by 25 micrograms now**, recheck TFTs in 4 weeks.

elim: Waiting risks maternal hypothyroidism during fetal brain development.
Requirements go up, not down.
Stopping harms mother and fetus.
PTU treats hyperthyroidism in pregnancy.

steps.x: **B. Increase by 25 micrograms and check TFTs in 4 weeks.** Even if euthyroid.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man is admitted drowsy and confused after being found at home in cold weather. He has hypothyroidism and has not collected his prescriptions for 3 months. His temperature is 33.6°C, pulse rate 44 bpm, BP 86/52 mmHg and respiratory rate 9 breaths per minute. A diagnosis of myxoedema coma is made.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV hydrocortisone and IV levothyroxine in ICU
practice.e: Myxoedema coma is managed in ICU with IV levothyroxine plus IV hydrocortisone (until adrenal insufficiency is excluded), supportive care and endocrine input. Oral replacement is too slow and unreliable.

steps.x: Initial management of a named emergency.
Hypothermic, bradycardic, hypotensive: critically unwell.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **ICU with IV hydrocortisone and IV levothyroxine.**

elim: Carbimazole and propranolol are for thyroid storm.
Oral absorption is unreliable in coma; route must be IV.
Oral low dose is for stable elderly patients, not coma.
Rewarming alone ignores the cause and he cannot go home.

steps.x: **B. IV hydrocortisone and IV levothyroxine in ICU.** Steroid cover until Addison's is excluded.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman has a 5 month history of tiredness, weight gain and constipation. Her pulse rate is 54 bpm and BP 130/84 mmHg. Investigations show a TSH of 19 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 of 6 pmol/L (9–23). Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are positive.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism for her raised TSH?
o: Autonomous TSH secretion from a pituitary adenoma
Increased hypothalamic TRH due to cold exposure
Loss of negative feedback from low thyroid hormone
practice.e: In primary hypothyroidism the failing gland makes less T4, removing negative feedback on the pituitary, so TSH rises. TSH receptor antibodies cause Graves'.

steps.x: Mechanism of one lab result.
Primary Hashimoto's hypothyroidism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Low T4 means **less negative feedback**, so the pituitary pushes out more TSH.

elim: A TSH-secreting adenoma would give a high T4.
Cold exposure is not the driver here; the gland is failing.
Renal clearance is not the mechanism.
TSH receptor antibodies cause Graves' and suppress TSH.

steps.x: **C. Loss of negative feedback.** High TSH + low T4 = the gland is the problem.

prompts.q: What are the causes of hypothyroidism worldwide and in the UK?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the setting (developed vs developing) and the drug list decide the cause.

points.why: Most common globally, e.g. Africa, Asia, South America.
Also the most common cause in children.
Common after treating Graves'.
Always scan the drug list in a stem.

prompts.q: List the symptoms and signs of hypothyroidism.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: everything slows down. Name the specific signs as well as the vague symptoms.

points.why: The opposite of thyrotoxicosis.
Menorrhagia can co-exist with iron deficiency.

points.p: Delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes
points.why: The classic 'most likely examination finding'.

points.p: Hertoghe sign: loss of the lateral third of the eyebrows
points.why: Also called Queen Anne's sign.

points.p: Dry skin, hair loss, hoarse voice, periorbital puffiness, goitre
points.why: Myxoedema deposits cause the puffiness and hoarseness.
A recognised association.

prompts.q: What conditions are associated with Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one autoimmune disease in the stem should make you look for another.

points.why: Shared HLA-DR3/DR5 susceptibility.
Consider if levothyroxine absorption is poor.
Addison's matters: steroids before thyroxine in crisis.
Goitre from lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltration.

prompts.q: What is myxoedema coma, how does it present and what precipitates it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: hypothermia plus bradycardia plus reduced consciousness in a thyroid patient.

points.why: Can progress to heart and respiratory failure.
The coma may only be drowsiness.
Thyroid storm is the hot, fast opposite.

points.p: Precipitants: infection, cold, stopping thyroid replacement
points.why: Stems often mention winter and a missed prescription.

prompts.q: What TFT patterns show primary, subclinical and secondary hypothyroidism?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: read TSH first, then free T4.

points.p: Primary: high TSH, low free T4
points.why: TFTs are the gold standard.

points.p: Subclinical: high TSH, normal free T4
points.why: Usually no symptoms.

points.p: Secondary (pituitary): low or normal TSH, low T4
points.why: A 'normal' TSH can hide pituitary failure.

points.p: High TSH with low-normal T4 on treatment: poor adherence
points.why: Ask about how and when tablets are taken.

prompts.q: How is levothyroxine treatment monitored, and how is subclinical disease followed up?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the numbers 4–6 weeks and 3–6 months are both tested.

points.p: Recheck TFTs 4–6 weeks after any dose change
points.why: TSH half-life is 4–6 weeks.

points.p: TSH low: reduce dose; TSH high: increase dose
points.why: Titrate to TSH.
Confirms persistence before treating.

points.p: Then TPO antibodies (positive = higher progression risk)
points.why: First-line further test in subclinical disease.

prompts.q: What is the first-line treatment and which patients need extra caution?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the drug, the start dose and who gets a low start.

points.p: Levothyroxine, starting around 25 mcg daily, titrated by TSH
points.why: Carbimazole and PTU are for overactive glands.

points.p: Caution in elderly and IHD: angina, arrhythmia
points.why: Start low, go slow.

points.p: Raises osteoporosis and fracture risk in menopausal women
points.why: Avoid over-replacement.

points.p: Pregnancy: increase by 25 mcg when confirmed, TFTs in 4 weeks
points.why: Even if euthyroid.

prompts.q: Which drugs interact with levothyroxine, and when is subclinical hypothyroidism treated?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a TSH that will not come down in an adherent patient is an interaction.

points.p: Ferrous sulphate: levothyroxine first, iron 2–4 hours later
points.why: Low MCV and tiredness: suspect co-existing iron deficiency.

points.p: Calcium, digoxin, HRT: space by 4 hours
points.why: All reduce or alter absorption.

points.p: Over 80s with TSH 5.5–10: watch and wait
points.why: Mild TSH rise is normal with ageing.

points.p: Under 65, TSH 5.5–10, symptomatic, raised twice 3 months apart: 6-month trial
points.why: Also treat if TSH over 10, antibodies positive or pregnancy planned.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: two IV drugs, one location.

points.why: Ventilatory and circulatory support may be needed.
Oral absorption is unreliable.

points.p: IV hydrocortisone until adrenal insufficiency excluded
points.why: Thyroxine alone can unmask an adrenal crisis.
High mortality emergency.

prompts.q: Why does Hashimoto's cause hypothyroidism, and why is TSH raised?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the antibodies, the cells and the feedback loop.

points.why: TSH receptor antibodies are Graves'.
The infiltrate causes the goitre.
Stored hormone leaks from damaged follicles.

points.p: Low T4 removes negative feedback, so TSH rises
points.why: A pituitary cause gives a low TSH.

prompts.q: Why does hypothyroidism cause bradycardia, constipation and delayed reflexes?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: less thyroid hormone, slower metabolism in each tissue.

points.p: Reduced heart rate and myocardial contractility
points.why: Thyroid hormone normally sensitises the heart to catecholamines.
Hence constipation.
Delayed relaxation, not reduced contraction.
Explains cold intolerance and weight gain.

glossary.Hypothyroidism: Underactive thyroid: too little thyroid hormone, so metabolism slows across the body.
glossary.Hashimoto's: Autoimmune thyroiditis where antibodies and lymphocytes destroy the thyroid; the most common UK cause of hypothyroidism.
glossary.Anti-TPO: Antibodies against thyroid peroxidase, an enzyme that makes thyroid hormone; positive in about 90% of Hashimoto's.
glossary.TPO antibodies: Antibodies against thyroid peroxidase; positive in Hashimoto's and predict progression of subclinical disease.
glossary.Thyroglobulin: Protein stored in thyroid follicles from which T4 and T3 are made; antibodies to it occur in Hashimoto's.
glossary.TSH: Thyroid-stimulating hormone from the pituitary; rises when thyroid hormone is low (primary hypothyroidism).
glossary.TRH: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus that tells the pituitary to release TSH.
glossary.Free T4: Unbound thyroxine in the blood, the active measured thyroid hormone level.
glossary.T3: Triiodothyronine, the most active thyroid hormone, mostly made by converting T4 in tissues.
glossary.TFTs: Thyroid function tests: TSH and free T4, the gold standard for diagnosing thyroid disease.
glossary.Subclinical hypothyroidism: Raised TSH with normal free T4 and usually no symptoms.
glossary.Secondary hypothyroidism: Thyroid underactivity caused by pituitary failure, so TSH is low or inappropriately normal.
glossary.Levothyroxine: Synthetic T4 tablet, first-line replacement treatment for hypothyroidism.
glossary.Liothyronine: Synthetic T3; faster acting and not first-line for hypothyroidism.
glossary.Carbimazole: Antithyroid drug that blocks hormone synthesis; used for hyperthyroidism, never for hypothyroidism.
glossary.Myxoedema: Thickened, puffy skin and tissues from glycosaminoglycan deposits in severe hypothyroidism.
glossary.Myxoedema coma: Life-threatening decompensated hypothyroidism with hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension and reduced consciousness.
glossary.Hertoghe sign: Loss of the outer (lateral) third of the eyebrows, a sign of hypothyroidism.
glossary.Queen Anne's sign: Another name for Hertoghe sign: loss of the lateral third of the eyebrows.
glossary.Goitre: Enlargement of the thyroid gland, seen as a neck swelling.
glossary.Deep tendon reflexes: Muscle jerks on tapping a tendon, such as the ankle or knee jerk.
glossary.Carpal tunnel syndrome: Compression of the median nerve at the wrist causing tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers.
glossary.Tinel's sign: Tapping over a nerve reproduces tingling in its distribution; positive at the wrist in carpal tunnel syndrome.
glossary.Bradycardia: Heart rate below 60 beats per minute.
glossary.Hashitoxicosis: Brief hyperthyroid phase early in Hashimoto's as damaged follicles release stored hormone.
glossary.HLA-DR3: Immune gene type linked to several autoimmune diseases, including Hashimoto's and type 1 diabetes.
glossary.Amiodarone: Iodine-rich antiarrhythmic drug that can cause hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism.
glossary.Lithium: Mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder that can cause hypothyroidism and goitre.
glossary.Radioiodine: Radioactive iodine treatment that destroys thyroid tissue; often leads to hypothyroidism.
glossary.Ferrous sulphate: Oral iron tablet that reduces levothyroxine absorption if taken together.
glossary.Hydrocortisone: Steroid given IV in myxoedema coma to cover possible adrenal insufficiency.
glossary.Adrenal insufficiency: Too little cortisol from the adrenal glands, as in Addison's disease.
glossary.Negative feedback: When a hormone switches off the signal that made it; T4 normally suppresses TSH.
glossary.NG145: NICE guideline on assessing and managing thyroid disease.
glossary.IHD: Ischaemic heart disease: narrowed coronary arteries reducing blood flow to the heart muscle.
glossary.MCV: Mean cell volume, the average red cell size; low in iron deficiency.
glossary.Sick euthyroid syndrome: Abnormal thyroid tests in acutely ill patients whose thyroid gland is actually normal.
